Article Title: 'India-France relations reached new heights': PM Modi virtually inaugurates BAPS Temple in Paris
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday hailed India-France relations, saying that the strategic partnership between the two countries is particularly special because it rests on the solid foundation of long-standing cultural and political ties.Addressing the inauguration of the Swaminarayan temple in Paris, Modi hoped that the grand temple would stand for centuries as a symbol of cooperation and opportunity between the two nations.“In recent years, relations between India and France have reached new heights. Together with my friend, President (Emmanuel) Macron, both nations are building a Special Global Strategic Partnership,” he said.The Prime Minister said the inauguration was more than a religious or architectural occasion, asserting that it embodied the spirit of universal brotherhood and the ancient Indian philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam.“Today, this stage has become an awakened platform for the spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam,” he said. PM Modi also underlined that the establishment of temples and the spread of India's spiritual traditions overseas also carry with them the country's philosophical message of human unity. Referring to the ideal that minds should be united and hearts connected, he said India's civilisational thought has a universal appeal.PM Modi also placed the inauguration in the wider context of the rapidly expanding India-France partnership, noting that New Delhi and Paris were working together to build what he described as a Special Global Strategic Partnership.“We are also celebrating 2026 as the India-France Year of Innovation. This strategic partnership is particularly special because it rests on the solid foundation of our long-standing cultural and political ties,” he said.“Both countries are building a Special Global Strategic Partnership together,” he said, while recalling his cooperation with French President Emmanuel Macron.PM Modi said history bears witness that the sacrifice of Indian soldiers in France remains alive in the hearts of people to this day.“Language enthusiasts also know the pivotal role French scholars played in popularising Sanskrit. Romain Rolland’s writings on Ramakrishna Paramahamsa and Swami Vivekananda brought our societies closer,” he said.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi hails India-France relations, saying strategic partnership rests on the solid foundation of long-standing cultural and political ties. Addressing the inauguration of the Swaminarayan temple in Paris, Modi hoped that the grand temple would stand for centuries as a symbol of cooperation and opportunity.

Article Title: Amazon techie leaves Rs 46 lakh package to join Indian Army, set to be commissioned at OTA Gaya
Article Text:
Shardendu Tiwari





LUCKNOW: Lucknow’s 27-year-old Shardendu Tiwari, who worked as a cloud engineer at Amazon with an annual package of around Rs 46 lakh, is set to be commissioned into the Army at the Officers Training Academy (OTA), Gaya, on Saturday.A second-generation soldier, Shardendu chose military service after leaving behind a corporate career and an opportunity with global aerospace company Airbus. His commissioning will mark the culmination of his journey from the technology sector to the armed forces.Shardendu resides in Neelmatha, Lucknow, and his family traces its roots to Pipergaon in Sultanpur district. His father, Honorary Captain Raj Kumar Tiwari, served in the Army Service Corps for 36 years before retiring. Inspired by his father, Shardendu developed an inclination towards joining the armed forces during his childhood.He completed his schooling at Kendriya Vidyalaya, Chandimandir, Haryana. He pursued a Bachelor of Engineering degree in Information Technology and later completed an MTech in Computer Science and Information Security from Punjab Engineering College, Chandigarh.Shardendu appeared for Army selection eight times before succeeding.He joined through the technical entry route, which enabled him to serve in the Army while remaining connected with technology.“I was also drawn to the armed forces because of the opportunities they offer for adventure and field service,” he said.During training at OTA Gaya, his leadership qualities earned him the appointment of Senior Under Officer (SUO), one of the highest cadet appointments at the academy. He enjoys playing basketball and table tennis.
Article Summary: Shardendu Tiwari, 27, is set to be commissioned into the Army at the Officers Training Academy (OTA), Gaya, on Saturday. His commissioning will mark the culmination of his journey from the technology sector to the armed forces. Shardendu chose military service after leaving behind a corporate career and opportunity with global aerospace company Airbus.

Article Title: UN-backed map must depict India's territory accurately: Govt
Article Text:
UN-backed map must depict India's territory accurately: Govt

MEA: Resolution doesn't endorse any specific map

NEW DELHI: After endorsing a UN General Assembly resolution on equal-area world map, the govt warned Sunday that the proposed new map must depict India's sovereign territory, including the Union territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, in accordance with India's official map and any inaccurate or misleading depiction would be unacceptable."Our position on India's sovereignty and territorial integrity is clear, consistent and non-negotiable," said MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, replying to media queries.India was among the 164 countries that voted in favour of UN General Assembly's Sept 4 resolution, "Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World's Regions, Particularly Africa".MEA said the resolution's purpose is to encourage the use of equal-area map projections that preserve the relative sizes of continental landmasses, and it neither adopts nor authenticates any particular world map, nor does it address political cartography, including international boundaries, disputed territories or place names."India voted in favour of the resolution and also made an explanation, stressing the underlying principle of promoting equal-area cartographic representation.We also highlighted that the resolution does not constitute endorsement of any specific map, projection or depiction of national boundaries," said Randhir Jaiswal.The resolution received abstentions from Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine, and a lone vote against it from US.The resolution noted that the Mercator projection remains widely used in educational, media, digital and official materials, despite the considerable distortion of landmasses to the North and South, far from the equator.It expressed concern that this distortion contributed to minimising the perceived sizes of Africa, Latin America and South Asia, and perpetuating an unbalanced view of the world. India welcomed the intention behind the resolution to promote more accurate and representative cartographic practices.
Article Summary: UN-backed map must depict India's territory accurately: Govt. MEA: Resolution doesn't endorse any specific map or depiction of national boundaries. India was among the 164 countries that voted in favour of UN General Assembly's Sept 4 resolution, "Correct the Map"

Article Title: The annual Delhi Yamuna flood threat- why September matters?
Article Text:
2025: People, animals living near floodplains relocated on roads ( on left); Yamuna Flood plain board (on right) (Pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)

Delhi’s real test: Preparing before the next flood

A year after the Yamuna inundated large parts of Delhi, the river is again flowing above the danger mark. The immediate threat may be lower this time, but heavy rain in the upper catchment could quickly change the picture, exposing how vulnerable the city’s floodplain still remains.That vulnerability is built into Delhi’s geography. Every monsoon, as September sets in, the city watches the Yamuna closely because even a sharp rise in the river or a sudden surge in upstream discharge can quickly put thousands living and working along the floodplains at risk.The danger mark at the Old Iron Railway Bridge is 205.33 metres, while evacuation of vulnerable residents begins when the river reaches around 206 metres. On September 6, the Yamuna was flowing at 205.59 metres, already slightly above the danger mark.And it is not just the people living along the river who feel the impact. When the Yamuna rises sharply, critical roads and infrastructure can also be affected. The Loha Pul, a vital link between Central Delhi (including Kashmere Gate and Old Delhi Railway Station) and East Delhi, is among the key crossings vulnerable to rising waters during severe floods.Last year, the warning turned into a full-blown crisis.The Yamuna crossed the danger mark and rose above 207 metres, inundating several low-lying parts of the Capital and forcing more than 10,000 people to evacuate vulnerable areas.The impact extended well beyond flooded homes. Roads and public infrastructure were affected, electricity supplies were disrupted and houses were left covered in mud and silt after the water receded. Thousands whose livelihoods depended on the floodplain also took a hit.Floodwaters reached the Ring Road and Outer Ring Road, disrupting traffic between Majnu ka Tilla and the Salimgarh bypass. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi stopped cremations at Nigambodh Ghat and the Geeta Colony ground because of flooding. Water-treatment infrastructure was also affected.A major factor was the enormous volume of water released from the Hathnikund Barrage in Haryana after intense rainfall in the upper Yamuna catchment.A year later, attention is once again turning to the Yamuna.The monsoon remains active, with heavy rain reported in parts of Delhi and northern India. The immediate concern is not simply the river’s current level, but how much water is being released upstream and whether intense rainfall in the catchment pushes those levels sharply higher.The Yamuna has remained comparatively stable this year, despite crossing the danger mark.Dr Shiv Singh Rawat, water expert and convener of the WalkForYamuna Campaign, said the difference becomes clearer when the upstream discharge is examined. “This year’s situation needs to be understood in its proper hydrological context. The maximum discharge released from Hathnikund Barrage during this year was around 64,000 cusecs, which is significantly below an extreme flood situation. That helps explain why Delhi experienced a much less severe river-flood situation than in 2025. ”But that relative stability offers no guarantee.The India Meteorological Department has warned of isolated heavy rainfall over Haryana, Chandigarh and Delhi from September 10-12.Fairly widespread rain, accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning, is also likely over Uttarakhand from September 6-12, while rainfall disturbances are expected over Himachal Pradesh.For Delhi, what happens upstream can matter as much as what happens within the Capital itself.A spell of intense rainfall in the upper catchment can send a surge downstream, leaving communities along the floodplain with limited time to respond.The relatively stable Yamuna this year may have given Delhi a temporary reprieve, but the underlying vulnerability remains.The floodplain is not simply vacant land beside the river.It acts as a natural buffer during floods, helps recharge groundwater and performs an important ecological function.“The 2-km-stretch on both sides of Yamuna acts as a buffer for floods, restores groundwater balance and acts as an organic filter. However, excess rain will create flooding in Delhi, and sanitation is not adequate to handle floods in the Capital,” says environmentalist Kavita Ashok.Rawat warns that the greater danger could emerge gradually through construction and development. “The concern is that areas outside the most restrictive floodplain zones could gradually become corridors for permanent construction, infrastructure and commercial riverfront activity,” he says. “That would undermine the very floodplain functions that protect the city.”The question, therefore, is not only whether the Yamuna will rise this September. It is whether Delhi is becoming more or less vulnerable when it does.For families living along Delhi’s floodplain, the monsoon is not simply a season of heavy rain. It is a recurring threat of displacement.When the river rises, families may have to move their belongings, livestock and essentials to higher ground with little warning.The granddaughter of Ramu Sahni, who lives with his family near the Yamuna floodplain, told TOI that residents don’t receive any advance warning.“We receive no warning on time. We see the rise in the water level of Yamuna and ourselves decide to shift to the roads with all our belongings. The authorities then notice the crowd on the roads and help us with tents.”Sahni, who came to Delhi from Bihar in search of employment many years ago, says the relief arrangements have also changed. “Earlier, they used to provide us with some ration and water in tents but now the situation has changed,” he says. “I don’t live here for free, I pay rent.”For many residents, simply relocating permanently is not an easy option.Their lives are tied to the floodplain through work, transport, markets and social networks. When the water recedes, they return.“We return back here when the water recedes after 2 months. This is all we have. I run a rickshaw, we are mostly ragpickers. Where will we go?”That cycle of evacuation, waiting, returning and rebuilding has become part of life for many families.For families with livestock, evacuation is even more complicated.Leaving home is one thing. Moving buffaloes, cattle, calves and other animals to safety is another. Stray animals are even more vulnerable, particularly when rising water cuts off their escape routes.Sahni says livestock is not simply property for floodplain families, it is their livelihood. “People usually take their buffaloes with them on the roads. How will they earn? Now they have installed fencing around a small Yamuna pond here. How will buffaloes go there? They need to be there for survival. If a flood comes right now, there is no way we can rescue them immediately as there is only a small route to travel.”When asked who rescues stray animals during floods, he had no clear answer.PETA India told TOI that animals stranded during floods can face exhaustion, dehydration, hunger, injury and drowning, making rapid rescue and access to food, clean water and veterinary care critical.“The biggest challenge when trying to reach animals in emergency situations is getting to them in the first place. Access may be cut off by rising water, for instance,” said Sachin Bangera of PETA India.During last year’s floods, PETA India’s Rapid Response Team arranged a boat to rescue dogs stranded in flooded areas and at risk of drowning.“Animals who are left chained are the most vulnerable because they cannot escape, or they become exhausted and drown,” Bangera said.Aditi Bakshi, Animal Welfare Advocate and Specialist - Government and Public Policy at Mercy For Animals, says the problem goes deeper than rescue.“Many people are forced into an impossible choice by a system that gives them no option. Rescue boats and relief camps do not take animals. When the administration tells a family to evacuate and will not let them bring their cow, their pigs, or their two goats, the family has to choose between their children’s safety and the animal’s life.”She argues that flood preparedness must explicitly include animals.According to Bakshi, Delhi lacks a comprehensive operational framework covering animal evacuation, including a nodal officer, mapped animal shelters, pre-monsoon fodder stocks, evacuation protocols for large animals and regular drills. “A plan that has never been drilled is not a plan; it is a document,” she says.For Delhi’s floodplain residents, the Yamuna may rise for only a few days. The disruption can last months.That makes flood preparedness about far more than issuing warnings once the river begins to rise.“Relief must be immediate, but rehabilitation must be humane and sustainable. People should not have to repeatedly rebuild their lives every monsoon,” says Dr Heera Lal Patel, IAS.During a flood emergency, he says, authorities need to provide clear information, accessible evacuation routes, transport and safe shelters. Vulnerable families cannot be expected to organise an evacuation on their own.Rawat argues that Delhi needs scientifically determined, risk-based floodplain zoning.“The real measures of success are: how many people are taken out of high-risk locations, flood-storage capacity restored and new encroachment prevented.”For companion-animal guardians, PETA India recommends identifying safe locations where pets will be accepted, keeping an emergency kit ready, and ensuring animals are microchipped or wear collars with updated contact details.But the larger challenge is institutional.The Yamuna’s rise is predictable. The exact scale and timing of a flood may not be.For communities living beside the river, that distinction can mean the difference between having time to evacuate and scrambling for safety as the water arrives.And every September, Delhi faces the same question: when the Yamuna rises again, will the city be better prepared, or will thousands once again be forced to leave their lives behind?
Article Summary: A year after the Yamuna inundated large parts of Delhi, the river is again flowing above the danger mark. The immediate threat may be lower this time, but heavy rain in the upper catchment could quickly change the picture. The danger mark at the Old Iron Railway Bridge is 205.33 metres.

Article Title: Isro will never be privatised, its role won't be diminished: Space Agency & INSPACe chief
Article Text:
Isro dismisses privatisation speculation, says role will only strengthen

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is the most important focus for Isro in the future? Advanced R&D Human spaceflight Next-generation launch systems 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI/BENGALURU: Allaying the fears of some of its staff that the organisation will be privatised and its role reduced to an R&D lab, Isro Sunday dismissed “speculation” about any diminution of its role as “misinformation”.“These assertions are completely baseless and incorrect. We wish to categorically state that Isro will neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished,” it said.Isro further said it would continue to remain “India’s principal institution for advanced space research and technology development, national and strategic missions, space science and exploration, and critical and frontier space capabilities”.Space promoter and regulator Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (INSPACe) chairperson Pawan Goenka also said Sunday that Isro would “remain the bedrock of the Indian space sector” and at the core of India’s space programme leading frontier research and the next generation of national missions like the space station and Gaganyaan.The agency said, “Participation of private sector in space is not about reducing its role.It is about enabling Isro to focus even more strongly on the next generation of India’s space programme, while industry scales mature technologies and capabilities. What is changing is not the importance of Isro, but the scale and structure of India’s space ecosystem. The transition is therefore towards an Isro-led national space ecosystem. ”The agency also said its role would progressively strengthen in areas where “its scientific expertise matters most: frontier R&D, advanced technologies, human spaceflight, next-generation launch systems, deep-space and planetary missions and strategic national capabilities. It will continue developing cutting-edge technologies, including advanced payloads for communication, navigation and Earth observation, sensors, propulsion systems and other critical technologies”.After nine Isro staff associations representing thousands sought clarification from the agency chairperson on the private sector shift, Goenka said on X, “Let me say it unequivocally: Isro’s role is by no means diminishing.”On scaling up the production of rockets and satellites in India, the INSPACe director declared that the country had set an “ambitious target” of 50 launches a year by 2030. “A goal of this scale cannot be achieved by one organisation alone. Govt and private industry have to build this future together,” he said.The INSPACe chairperson said, “The reforms since 2020 are about expanding India’s overall space ecosystem. IN-SPACe will facilitate and authorise greater non-govt participation, while NSIL will help commercialise mature capabilities.”Goenka said the idea of space reforms is to “let industry increasingly manufacture and scale mature launch vehicles, satellites and other systems, while Isro focuses on what it is uniquely placed to do: advanced R&D, scientific missions, strategic missions, new technologies, and infrastructure that is too complex for the private sector to develop on its own”.Assuring staff that they were going to handle big projects, he said, “Isro will remain at the core of India’s space programme, leading frontier research and the next generation of national missions, including Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035, an Indian crewed mission to the Moon by 2040, next-generation launch systems, and sustained lunar and planetary exploration.”“The direction is not a smaller Isro. It is a larger Indian space ecosystem, with Isro pushing the technological frontier,” he added.
Article Summary: Isro dismisses privatisation speculation, says role will only strengthen. Isro will remain at the core of India’s space programme, leading frontier research and the next generation of national missions. “A goal of this scale cannot be achieved by one organisation alone. Govt and private industry have to build this future together”

Article Title: What does the law say about inheritance? Know your rights
Article Text:
What can a daughter, wife, widow or mother legally claim?

Inheritance rights

Hindu women: Daughter has equal coparcenary rights

Muslim women: Share depends on the family structure

Christian women: Sons and daughters inherit equally

Parsi women: Daughter does not lose out to son

What happens when there is no will

Inheritance rights of women in India.

What if there is a will — but the daughter gets nothing

Legal steps to challenge a will

How can one challenge an unfair will

What if a woman is denied her share in property

What if the family says she has already given up her share

stridhan

So, what is a woman’s share in family property

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For generations, inheritance in India has been shaped by family relationships, religious personal laws and the nature of the property being inherited.A daughter may have an equal right with her brother in one situation, but not necessarily in another. A widow may be entitled to a share in her husband's estate, while a woman may also own property in her own right through inheritance, gifts or other means.The biggest question often arises when a person dies without leaving a will. In such cases, known as intestate succession, the applicable law determines who inherits and in what proportion. The rules differ across religious communities.The Hindu Succession Act, 1956, governs succession among Hindus and also applies to Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs, subject to its provisions. Muslims are generally governed by Muslim personal law on intestate succession, while Christians and Parsis are principally covered by the Indian Succession Act, 1925.So what can a woman legally claim?One of the biggest changes to women's inheritance rights came with the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005. It made a daughter a coparcener by birth in a Hindu joint family governed by Mitakshara law, giving her the same rights and liabilities as a son.The Supreme Court's 2020 judgment in Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma clarified that this right is acquired by birth and does not depend on whether the father was alive when the 2005 amendment came into force.Marriage also does not take away a daughter's coparcenary rights. However, an important distinction must be made between coparcenary property and a parent's self-acquired property.If a Hindu father dies intestate, leaving behind his wife, son and daughter, and the property is his self-acquired property, all three are Class I heirs. In a simple example involving property worth Rs 1 crore, the wife, son and daughter would each inherit about Rs 33.33 lakh.The calculation becomes more nuanced when the property is coparcenary property, explains advocate Rupali Jain.“If the Rs 1 crore is Mitakshara coparcenary property, the calculation is more nuanced. A notional partition is assumed immediately before the father's death. On the stated facts, assuming the father, one son and one daughter constitute the coparcenary and the wife is entitled to a share on such partition, the wife, son, daughter and father would each be attributed a one-fourth share, or Rs 25 lakh, for purposes of the hypothetical partition,” Jain said.The father's Rs 25 lakh share would then devolve equally among his Class I heirs, the wife, son and daughter. Each would receive an additional Rs 8.33 lakh. This means all three would ultimately receive approximately Rs 33.33 lakh.“The Supreme Court in Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v Hirabai Khandappa Magdum held that the fiction of notional partition must be carried through to its logical consequences and that the widow's share arising from the hypothetical partition cannot simply be ignored,” she added.Another common misconception is that every property owned by a parent is ancestral property in which children have a birthright. That is not necessarily so.Muslim inheritance in India operates under Muslim personal law, which does not follow the same joint-family property model.Islamic inheritance rules identify different categories of heirs and prescribe shares depending on which relatives survive the deceased. The applicable school of Muslim law can also matter.The daughter will generally receive half the son's share but the actual calculation depends on all the surviving heirs.A widow's share also depends on whether the deceased leaves descendants. Broadly, under commonly applied Sunni rules, a widow receives one-eighth where there are children or certain descendants and one-fourth where there are none."The share of a Muslim woman therefore has to be calculated based on the complete family structure," said advocate Pritish Sunil Teckchandani.Muslim testamentary succession is also different. Generally, a Muslim's power to make a will is restricted to one-third of the estate without the consent of the heirs, subject to applicable personal-law rules.For Christians, intestate succession is primarily governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925.Where a Christian man dies without a will leaving a widow and children, the widow receives one-third of the estate, while the remaining two-thirds goes equally to the children.For example, if a Christian man dies leaving a wife, one son and one daughter and an estate worth Rs 90 lakh, each would ordinarily receive Rs 30 lakh. "The widow and each child would ordinarily receive one-third each," said Teckchandani.The position changes depending on which relatives survive the deceased, but there is no distinction between sons and daughters in the straightforward situation described above.Unlike Hindu law, Christian succession has no equivalent concept of coparcenary rights by birth. A Christian daughter does not become a co-owner of her father's property merely because she is his daughter; her inheritance generally arises upon succession.Parsi intestate succession is governed by special provisions in Part V of the Indian Succession Act. The exact entitlement depends on the relatives who survive the deceased.Thus, where a Parsi man dies intestate leaving a widow, son and daughter, the son and daughter inherit on an equal footing under the applicable rules.The calculation can change where there are more children, a predeceased child, grandchildren or other specified relatives.When a person dies without a valid will, the property does not automatically go to the eldest son or the closest male relative. The applicable succession law determines who inherits.For Hindus, the Hindu Succession Act lays down a hierarchy of heirs. A widow, son, daughter and mother are among the Class I heirs of a Hindu man who dies intestate.For Muslims, inheritance is calculated under applicable Muslim personal-law rules rather than a Class I heir system.For Christians and Parsis, the relevant provisions of the Indian Succession Act apply.This is why there is no single formula for a woman's inheritance in India. Her share can depend on her religion, relationship to the deceased, the relatives who survive, the nature of the property and whether there is a valid will.“For self-acquired property, a Hindu father can generally leave the entire property to his son and exclude his daughter through a valid Will. A daughter has no compulsory share in such property merely by virtue of being his daughter,” said Tekchandani.This is where the nature of the property becomes particularly important.A person can generally make a will determining how property that they legally own and can dispose of should be distributed. Therefore, a Hindu father can ordinarily leave his entire self-acquired property to his son and exclude his daughter."The daughter has no compulsory share in such property merely by virtue of being his daughter," said Teckchandani.But a will cannot simply wipe out another person's existing coparcenary interest. A daughter who already has a coparceny share cannot be deprived of that existing interest merely through her father's will."An unfair will is not necessarily an invalid will," explained Teckchandani. However, a woman can challenge a will if there are grounds to question its validity. These can include forgery, lack of testamentary capacity, coercion, undue influence, improper execution or other suspicious circumstances.Jain said courts may examine factors such as whether the testator was elderly, ill or dependent on the beneficiary, whether the beneficiary isolated the testator from other family members, whether there was a sudden departure from an earlier will, or whether the beneficiary was involved in preparing or executing the document."The person alleging coercion must produce credible evidence; mere suspicion or the fact that one child received substantially more property is generally insufficient," said Jain.Medical records, previous wills, messages, bank documents and testimony from doctors, neighbours, lawyers and attesting witnesses may become important evidence.The first step is to establish what the will says and what property it covers.A woman challenging a will should obtain the will, death certificate and relevant property documents. If probate or letters of administration proceedings are pending, she can enter the proceedings and raise objections."If probate proceedings are filed, enter appearance/file objections or a caveat, after which the proceeding becomes contentious," explained Jain.If no such proceedings are pending, the appropriate civil remedy will depend on the circumstances.The court can examine whether the will was properly executed and attested, whether the deceased had testamentary capacity and whether there was fraud, coercion, undue influence or another circumstance affecting its validity.The first step is to establish the property's ownership and character. Sale deeds, title documents, mutation records, partition deeds, gift or settlement deeds, wills and other records can help determine what a woman is actually entitled to.Depending on the dispute, a woman may approach a civil court seeking remedies such as partition and separate possession, declaration of rights, cancellation of an invalid document or an injunction.One of the biggest risks comes when family members ask a daughter to sign a release deed, relinquishment deed, family settlement, partition document or NOC without fully understanding its consequences."The biggest mistake is giving up legal rights informally in the name of maintaining family relations, without understanding the property's character or documenting the settlement," said Jain.A woman should determine whether the property is self-acquired, inherited or coparcenary, establish her legal share and obtain independent advice before signing away any interest.A daughter may be told that she has no claim because she is married, that her brother "needs the property", or that her share was already given to her through wedding expenses orWhether a woman has actually relinquished a property right depends on the applicable law and whether there is a legally valid document or transaction establishing that relinquishment."Family pressure can make people sign documents simply to avoid conflict, but such documents can have significant and sometimes irreversible consequences," said Teckchandani. A verbal family understanding and a legally valid relinquishment or settlement document are not necessarily the same thing.Well, there is no single answer to this question.For a Hindu woman, a daughter can have equal coparcenary rights with a son, while inheritance of self-acquired property after an intestate death follows a different calculation.For a Muslim woman, the share depends on the applicable personal law and the complete family structure. For Christian and Parsi women, succession is principally governed by the Indian Succession Act, with sons and daughters generally treated equally in the relevant intestate situations.A will can also change the outcome, particularly when it concerns property that the testator was free to dispose of. But a will that is unequal is not automatically invalid, nor can it simply extinguish an existing legal interest such as a coparcenary share.For women facing an inheritance dispute, the key questions are therefore: What personal law applies? Who survived the deceased? What kind of property is involved? Was there a valid will? Was the property already transferred or partitioned? And has the woman actually and legally relinquished her share?Knowing the answers to those questions is often the difference between walking away from property and successfully asserting a legal claim.
Article Summary: Inheritance in India has been shaped by family relationships, religious personal laws and the nature of the property being inherited. A widow may be entitled to a share in her husband's estate. A woman may also own property in her own right through inheritance, gifts or other means.

Article Title: Isro says its 'next chapter' is leading national space ecosystem
Article Text:
ISRO “would neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished”.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Two days after nine employee bodies at Isro centres sought written clarity on the future role of the organisation amid space-sector reforms, Isro on Sunday hinted at its “next chapter” while categorically stating that it “would neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished”.“Isro will continue to remain India’s principal institution for advanced space R&D, national and strategic missions, space science and exploration, and critical and frontier space capabilities. Participation of the private sector is not about reducing Isro’s role. It is about enabling Isro to focus even more strongly on the next generation of India’s space programme, while industry scales mature technologies and capabilities,” Isro said.Also read: Isro will remain ‘bedrock of Indian space sector’, says Goenka What is changing is not the importance of Isro, but the scale and structure of India’s space ecosystem, it said, adding that the space-sector reforms institutionalised through the Indian Space Policy 2023, along with progressive liberalisation of FDI policy, aim to create a larger, stronger and globally competitive Indian space ecosystem.“Industry, start-ups and academia are being enabled to participate across the space value chain, complementing and multiplying Isro’s capabilities.The reforms should therefore be seen as ecosystem expansion and capability multiplication, not privatisation,” Isro said.As India’s industrial and technological capabilities have grown, mature and scalable activities can increasingly be undertaken by Indian industry, it said, adding Isro has already transferred multiple technologies to industry.“Transferring a mature technology doesn’t mean Isro is withdrawing from that domain. It enables large-scale production, commercialisation, innovation and access to global markets while allowing Isro’s scientific and technical manpower to concentrate on advanced research, next-generation technologies and complex national missions,” It said.The transition is therefore towards an “Isro-led national space ecosystem.” “...Isro’s role will progressively strengthen in areas where its scientific expertise matters most: frontier R&D, advanced technologies, human spaceflight, next-generation launch systems, deep-space and planetary missions and strategic national capabilities,” it said.The agency added that it’ll continue developing cutting-edge technologies, including advanced payloads for communication, navigation and Earth observation, sensors, propulsion systems and other critical technologies.“Meanwhile, mature and routinely manufactured systems can increasingly be scaled through industry. Production of mature launch vehicles, routine satellites and other established systems can increasingly be undertaken by industry or PSUs through appropriate competitive processes,” Isro said.This, it says, allows Isro to devote more resources and scientific manpower to the next generation of technologies and missions, while the wider ecosystem provides the investment, manufacturing capacity and scale required by an expanding national space programme.Pointing out that the transition was important in the context of Space Vision 2047, it said technologies needed for establishing the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035, crewed mission to Moon by 2040, developing next-generation and reusable launch systems, pursuing sustained lunar and planetary exploration, and establishing India as a major global space power, require Isro to remain focused on advanced research and capabilities that cannot simply be substituted by commercial activity.The objective is “therefore to enable industry to scale mature capabilities while Isro pushes India towards the next technological frontier”.“The Department of Space provides overall policy direction, Isro remains the core organisation for advanced R&D, technology development and national missions. IN-SPACe facilitates and authorises the participation of non-government entities, while NSIL undertakes commercialisation and industry-led utilisation of mature capabilities,” Isro said.It added that industry and start-ups contribute investment, innovation, manufacturing capacity and market access. “At the same time, ownership and control of critical national space infrastructure and strategic capabilities will continue to remain with the Govt. Private participation in operations and services will be enabled where appropriate and will remain subject to national-security, safety and other regulatory requirements. Strategic and nationally critical capabilities will continue to be governed by security, safety, quality and national-interest considerations,” it said.
Article Summary: Isro has hinted at its ‘next chapter’ while categorically stating that it “would neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished’ “Isro will continue to remain India’s principal institution for advanced space R&D, national and strategic missions, space science and exploration,” it said.

NEW DELHI: Uttarakhand waqf board's plan to introduce a revised marriage contract, or nikahnama, within a month "to align it with the Uniform Civil Code " has not gone down well with All India Muslim Personal Law Board (AIMPLB), which has challenged UCC in the high court.AIMPLB spokesperson SQR Ilyas said that the board opposes any such move by state waqf board and state govt and wants to reiterate that the nikahnama should not be revised till Uttarakhand HC gives its judgement. NEW DELHI: The Centre is in a tangle over Supreme Court's landmark judgement on "creamy layer" that paved the way for induction in the elite civil services of OBC candidates who had cleared the examinations over past ten years but were denied appointments.On Aug 25, govt approached the apex court seeking clarification on the Rohit Nathan judgement that laid down that "salary" could not be added to the "income" to determine if a candidate from a PSU background falls in the "creamy layer" - like it is done for OBCs from non-PSU families. Govt, while seeking that it be allowed to go ahead with allocation of service for Civil Services-2025 without implementing the Nathan judgement, also raised questions about the SC's definition of "creamy layer".But barely a week ago, Centre told Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) that it intended to execute the SC order of March 11. "A decision has been made to implement the decision in terms of the judgement rendered by SC in Union of India vs Rohit Nathan," the ASG told the principal bench of CAT.On Aug 19, CAT was hearing a contempt petition against Centre as an OBC candidate, Basant Singh, had sought that the bench enforce its earlier order for his induction in civil services.His case was similar to those of candidates in whose favour SC delivered the Nathan judgement."It is further submitted by the learned ASG that 56 similarly placed candidates are also being considered along with the applicant," CAT quoted the ASG as submitting. CAT put off the case based on Centre's undertaking that necessary steps were being taken to implement the Nathan judgement.The apparently contradictory stands taken by govt within a week's interval have disappointed OBC candidates who felt the SC judgement in March had ended their wait for induction in civil services.The case pertains to department of personnel and training (DoPT)'s differential implementation of the "creamy layer" criterion for OBCs from a PSU background and others. While, as per 1993 office memorandum, "salary" and "agricultural income" are not included in computing the "income" of a family, DoPT has been taking "salary" into consideration for candidates with parents in PSUs. Govt has cited the absence of "equivalence of posts" - categorising posts in PSUs, banks, universities, etc.as "Group A, B, C, D" - as the source of confusion.But, according to guidelines, while Group A and Group B are ineligible for quotas, others are eligible if their "annual income" does not exceed Rs 8 lakh.After a long wait, following orders by three high courts in support of the candidates, SC ruled in March that "salary" cannot be the criterion for determination of "creamy layer" for any category as per the 1993 judgement and that candidates who have suffered should be inducted in civil services.
Article Summary: Centre in a tangle over Supreme Court's landmark judgement on "creamy layer" That paved the way for induction in the elite civil services of OBC candidates. Govt sought clarification on the Rohit Nathan judgement that laid down that "salary" could not be added to the "income"

NEW DELHI: With vultures vanishing from nearly 72% of their historically known nesting sites across India, Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav Sunday called for persistent efforts to create 'Vulture Safe Zones' to aid species recovery in the wild.Known as Nature's most efficient scavengers, the vulture population has seen a sharp decline since the 1990s, mainly due to disruption in their food chain and veterinary use of diclofenac, an anti-inflammatory drug that was commonly administered to livestock across the country. NEW DELHI: New Delhi: With vultures vanishing from nearly 72% of their historically known nesting sites across India over the years, Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav on Sunday pitched for conservation of the nature’s most efficient scavengers and called for continued efforts to create Vulture Safe Zones.He said vulture-safe veterinary practices, safe food availability and technical capacity-building were needed to aid species recovery in the wild.Speaking at an International Vulture Awareness Day 2026 event in Panchkula, Haryana, Yadav urged veterinary professionals, livestock owners, local administrations and communities to support conservation and safe carcass-management practices.Vultures play a vital role in keeping ecosystems clean by feeding on decaying carcasses. Unlike predators, they rarely kill their own prey. Instead, they are scavengers that feed on carrion left behind by other animals. By removing dead animal matter, vultures help keep the environment clean and significantly reduce the risk of disease spreading.Vulture populations have fallen sharply since the 1990s, mainly because of disruption to their food chain and veterinary use of diclofenac, an anti-inflammatory drug commonly administered to livestock.Research found vultures feeding on carcasses of treated livestock suffered kidney failure and died.India has nine vulture species: white-rumped, long-billed, slender-billed, red-headed, Egyptian, Himalayan griffon, Eurasian griffon, cinereous and bearded vultures. They are found from the Himalayan range to Kerala.A pan-India assessment by Wildlife Institute of India scientists last year recorded only 120 active historical nesting sites among 425 documented in literature across 25 states. Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan accounted for about 63% of all vulture nests. Researchers also identified 93 new nesting locations, taking the total to 213, including 103 in protected areas.Conservation breeding of vultures is under way at centres in Pinjore, Haryana; Rajabha Khawa, West Bengal; and Rani, Assam.During 2025–26, Jatayu Conservation Breeding Centre in Pinjore housed 356 vultures, bred 35 chicks and released or contributed 87 birds for reintroduction, environment ministry said. It transferred 90 birds to other conservation-breeding institutions and trained 1,222 participants from 22 institutions.The centre, run jointly by Haryana Forest Department and Bombay Natural History Society, breeds white-rumped, long-billed and slender-billed vultures.
Article Summary: Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav called for continued efforts to create Vulture Safe Zones. Vulture populations have fallen sharply since the 1990s, mainly because of disruption to their food chain and veterinary use of diclofenac, an anti-inflammatory drug.

NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday said the Narendra Modi government has prepared a roadmap to make India drug-free by 2029, calling the fight against narcotics a national security priority.Addressing the media, Shah stated that the fight against narcotics has moved beyond isolated actions to become a coordinated national campaign.Shah said it was PM Modi’s objective that “drug-free youth power” would lead India towards Viksit Bharat by 2047. Article Title: What's cooking? A kitchen fix to cut dementia risk in old age
Article Text:

New Delhi: What if one of the simplest ways to keep the brain active later in life is already sitting in the kitchen? A six-year study from Japan has found that older adults who cooked at home at least once a week were less likely to develop dementia requiring long-term care than those who cooked less often.The population-based study followed 10,978 adults aged 65 years and older and recorded 1,195 cases of dementia during the six-year follow-up. After accounting for demographic, socioeconomic and health-related factors, men who cooked at least once a week had a 23% lower risk of dementia, while women had a 27% lower risk, compared with those who cooked less than once a week. The association was even stronger among people with low cooking skills. Among them, more frequent home cooking was associated with a 67% lower risk of dementia in older adults.The findings, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, were based on data from the Japan Gerontological Evaluation Study. Researchers assessed cooking frequency and skills at the beginning of the study and then tracked dementia requiring care through Japan's public long-term care insurance records.Dr (Col) Joy Dev Mukherji, chairman and head, neurology, Max Super Speciality Hospital, Saket, said cooking is a surprisingly complex activity from a neurological point of view. "It involves planning, attention, working memory, while also combining movement and sensory stimulation," he said. However, he cautioned against interpreting the findings as proof that cooking prevents dementia.“This was an observational study and does not prove that cooking prevents dementia. It is also possible that people in the early stages of cognitive decline may gradually stop cooking because of difficulties with planning and memory,” he said.Dr Manjari Tripathi, head of neurology at AIIMS, highlighted the social dimension of cooking, saying preparing meals with friends, family or the wider community could provide additional cognitive and social engagement. She also encouraged men to cook, saying the activity must not be viewed as restricted to women.Interestingly, the association was strongest among people with lower cooking skills, possibly because less experienced cooks engage more in planning and problem-solving. However, this was not established by the study. Doctors said the broader message is to remain engaged in meaningful activities involving learning, planning, movement and social interaction, rather than viewing cooking as a treatment for dementia.
Article Summary: Six-year study from Japan found older adults who cooked at home at least once a week were less likely to develop dementia requiring long-term care. The association was even stronger among people with low cooking skills. More frequent home cooking was associated with a 67% lower risk of dementia in older adults.

No. The NSE and BSE will remain open for regular trading on September 4. Investors can buy and sell shares and trade equity derivatives during normal market hours, as Janmashtami is not listed as a trading holiday in the 2026 market calendar.Unlike some festival holidays, there is also no settlement holiday for the stock market on September 4. Trading and the associated clearing and settlement processes will follow the regular schedule.The distinction is important. A trading holiday means the stock exchanges are shut, while a settlement holiday allows trading to continue but pauses the clearing and settlement of eligible trades. Neither applies to the NSE and BSE on Janmashtami this year.The festival does, however, coincide with bank holidays in several states, with closures varying by region.The next full trading holiday for the Indian stock market is September 14, 2026, for Ganesh Chaturthi.According to the exchange calendar, trading will remain closed on the following dates:
Article Summary: Krishna Janmashtami is observed on Friday, September 4. The NSE and BSE will remain open for regular trading on that day. The next full trading holiday for the Indian stock market is September 14, 2026, for Ganesh Chaturthi.

Article Title: Silver prices crash over 40% from Rs 4 lakh/kg high to Rs 2.35 lakh, but buyers are still staying away; bigger problem yet to arrive as 2,000 tonnes ordered by Indian dealers risk piling up
Article Text:
Traders and analysts have said that the slowdown in investment demand can be seen across silver exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bars and coins.

Silver Demand Weakens

Massive stockpiling of silver

Silver’s Spectacular Fall

(Disclaimer: Recommendations and views on the stock market, or any other asset classes or personal finance management tips given by experts and analysts are their own. These opinions do not represent the views of The Times of India.)

A huge crash in silver prices should have led to a revival in demand, but investors seem to be staying away. And this has raised a fresh worry ahead of the festive season.Silver refiners and bullion dealers are seeing their inventories build up as new investment demand for the metal weakens. The situation comes even as silver prices have dropped by more than 40% from their January peak of over Rs 4 lakh per kg. Uncertainty over a possible breakthrough in the US-Iran war and concerns about subdued industrial demand have added to the pressure.In Mumbai’s spot market, silver was trading at Rs 2.35 lakh per kg earlier this week.Traders and analysts have said that the slowdown in investment demand can be seen across silver exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bars and coins. Investors who bought the metal when prices were significantly higher are now sitting on substantial losses, making them hesitant to make fresh purchases despite the steep correction in prices!Also Read | A couple sold gold for Rs 20 lakh to buy a home, another family got Rs 80 lakh for a US degree and business: How Indians are unlocking value of idle gold sitting in their lockers "Investment demand for silver ETFs, bars and coins has come down. Internationally, prices are unlikely to cross $100 per troy ounce immediately unless the US-Iran war comes to an end. Silver prices are undervalued," Chirag Sheth, global business head, Public Gold Bullion (SG) Pte told ET. "The continuous war between US and Iran has impacted the solar industry, semiconductor industry and EV industry where silver is used. "The weak demand is also creating an inventory problem for domestic players.Indian bullion dealers and refiners have reportedly placed orders for around 2,000 tonnes of silver, which is currently in transit. The additional supplies have raised concerns over a further build-up in stocks. India imports around 7,000 tonnes of silver every year."With no new investors coming in and no immediate signs of prices going up, refiners and bullion dealers are facing a problem internationally as well as in domestic markets," said James Jose, president, Precious Metals Refiners Forum.Silver prices have fallen steadily over the past seven months, following an extraordinary rally that pushed the metal more than 300% higher year-on-year. In January, silver crossed Rs 4 lakh per kg on the Multi Commodity Exchange for the first time."The market is still digesting the aftermath of the speculation-driven frenzy, and this may be prompting investors to stay away after many of them incurred significant losses," said Carsten Menke, head, Next Generation Research, Julius Baer told ET.The outlook for industrial demand is adding to the pressure, with consumption expected to weaken. "A shift to cheaper alternatives, such as aluminium and copper, has started, and the growth outlook for Chinese solar module makers, which are the biggest industrial users of silver, is not as strong anymore," Menke said.The ongoing US-Iran war has added to the negative sentiment surrounding silver. If the conflict continues for an extended period, investors may remain cautious. At the same time, expectations of weaker industrial consumption could make a rapid rebound in silver prices difficult.Despite the sharp fall, some long-term investors are once again looking at silver as a way to diversify their portfolios."The market has taken full cognisance of the marked decline in silver prices in recent days. Some investors have shaved off their allocation, while others have prepared for fresh acquisition depending on their views and goals," said Nilanjan Dey, partner, Wishlist Capital.Dey said investors who have a time horizon of five years or longer may look at buying silver ETFs in a staggered manner instead of putting in a large amount at one go. Monthly or fortnightly investments could help spread out the purchase price and reduce the impact of short-term price movements.For first-time investors looking to add precious metals to their portfolios as a diversification from equities, ETFs can provide exposure without the need to hold or manage physical silver. However, Dey warned that investors with a shorter investment horizon should not assume that the recent decline automatically makes silver an attractive buying opportunity.
Article Summary: Silver refiners and bullion dealers are seeing their inventories build up as new investment demand for the metal weakens. Silver prices have dropped by more than 40% from their January peak of over Rs 4 lakh per kg. Uncertainty over a possible breakthrough in the US-Iran war and concerns about subdued industrial demand have added to the pressure.

Article Title: RAKSHA Document : India unveils 10-year ‘RAKSHA’ roadmap to expand global defence & security ties

India looks to expand strategic defence ties under new ‘RAKSHA’ framework

Four key pillars of India's defence diplomacy roadmap

Strategic partnerships: Deepening bilateral and multilateral security cooperation.

Senior officials attend release event

10 years.The document, unveiled at a special event in New Delhi, lays out a framework aimed at aligning India's national security objectives with proactive international cooperation, according to the ministry of defence.The strategic blueprint focuses on deepening bilateral and multilateral security ties, building capacity with friendly countries, promoting indigenous defence exports and Article Summary: The document lays out a framework aimed at aligning India's national security objectives with proactive international cooperation.
