Article Title: Activists slam Bengaluru's 1.5 lakh-crore ‘car-centric’ infra push
Article Text:
Activists criticize government infrastructure plans exceeding health and education budgets





BENGALURU: The govt’s plan to push the city’s infrastructure projects worth over Rs 1.5 lakh crore amounts to spending more than three times the state’s annual health and education budgets on projects that would primarily benefit private car users, CIVIC Bangalore trustee Kathyayini Chamaraj said Sunday.She criticised the govt for bypassing institutional scrutiny, including the approval process under the Bengaluru Metropolitan Land Transport Authority (BMLTA), for such projects.Speaking at a Save Bangalore Committee roundtable, she said the proposed tunnel road from Silk Board to Hebbal would benefit only a small section of the population. Citing studies, she said estimates suggested that fewer than one lakh cars would use the tunnel daily, raising questions over the viability of the project and the scale of the proposed investment.“Rs 1.5 lakh crore is more than the state’s health and education budgets combined. The annual budgets for health and education together do not even cross Rs 50,000 crore. The govt is planning to spend three times that amount on infrastructure that will benefit private cars in Bengaluru, not even the whole of Karnataka,” she said.“Section 4(1)(c) of the RTI Act requires the govt to publicise the facts and explain the rationale before taking up such projects.Objections have to be collated, recorded and placed before the cabinet. Due process also mandates BMLTA approval, but the BMLTA body itself has not been constituted,” she said.Senior advocate Hemalatha Mahishi criticised the now-withdrawn plan that would allow construction on up to 5% of public park land, saying green spaces such as Cubbon Park and Lalbagh were already facing encroachments and losing space for walkers.“Though the proposal has been temporarily withdrawn, it is bound to be reintroduced. We must oppose it politically and demand the chief minister’s direct intervention,” she said.Former Bangalore University geology professor TJ Renuka Prasad raised concerns over the geological and environmental risks of the proposed hard-rock tunnel, citing instances of landslides, structural failures and environmental damage associated with tunnel projects in similar terrains.Referring to discussions with the Cubbon Park authorities over the Parks Preservation Act, Prasad said responsibility was subsequently shifted to the tourism department.He criticised the response of top officials to citizen campaigns, saying public signatures and objections could not be dismissed as insignificant. He called for greater public participation and collective action against policy decisions affecting the city’s green spaces and environment.Others present at the roundtable included Save Bangalore Committee convener G Shashikumar, Karnataka Medical Service Centre president Dr Sudha Kamath and Karnataka Electrical Consumers’ Association secretary V Gnanamurthy.
Article Summary: CIVIC Bangalore trustee Kathyayini Chamaraj criticised the govt for bypassing institutional scrutiny. She said the proposed tunnel road from Silk Board to Hebbal would benefit only a small section of the population. Citing studies, she said estimates suggested that fewer than one lakh cars would use the tunnel daily.

Article Title: From resettlement colony to PG hub: How Satya Niketan was stretched beyond its limits
Article Text:
The original building norms allowed only ground and first floors

Poll Vote & Share your view Should there be stricter regulations on building constructions in resettlement colonies like Satya Niketan? Absolutely Somewhat Not necessary 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion





NEW DELHI: Satya Niketan, a resettlement colony in south Delhi, has undergone a dramatic transformation from a low-rise neighbourhood meant to house displaced families and labourers to one of the capital’s most densely built hubs to accommodate students.Developed by Delhi Development Authority (DDA) during the 1970s and ’80s, the colony was planned as modest housing for families with limited means. Its original layout was markedly different from that of neighbouring Shanti Niketan and Anand Niketan, which were built in the 1960s as upscale cooperative housing societies, largely for senior govt officials and affluent people.Satya Niketan and neighbouring Arakpur Bagh Mochi, in contrast, comprised much smaller plots and low-rise residential structures.According to former DDA planning commissioner Sabyasachi Das, the original building norms allowed the construction of only ground and first floors in Satya Niketan and such colonies. This restriction was also linked to the area’s proximity to the airport.“Instead of approving or sanctioning individual building layout plans, DDA gave a standard plan to each beneficiary in such colonies so that they would not have to hire an architect.But there were instances when people engaged local builders who tweaked the plans,” Das said.A DDA official said under an arrangement, such resettlement colonies were transferred to Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) after about 90% of the construction had been completed.The character of Satya Niketan began significantly changing after 1973, when University of Delhi established its South Campus across the road. With institutes, including Sri Venkateswara College, Jesus and Mary College and Atma Ram Sanatan Dharma College expanding, the locality became an attractive and convenient option for students looking for accommodation close to their campuses.The shift began relatively gradually, with locals renting out rooms to students. Over time, however, the growing demand for accommodation turned houses into commercial rental properties. “It all started with accommodating students as tenants by adding beds, tables and other facilities, besides creating common toilets to meet the requirements,” Das said.The shift accelerated as properties were expanded both vertically and horizontally without necessary permissions. Family homes were converted into paying guest (PG) accommodation and rental units, while additional floors and rooms were added to accommodate more students on the same plot.While Master Plan for Delhi-2021 recognised the growing demand for such accommodation and permitted hostels and PG facilities in residential plots abutting roads that met specified right of way (ROW) requirements for mixed-use streets, residents said the prescribed norms, particularly those relating to road width, have often not been followed.The proposed Master Plan for Delhi-2047 has further simplified certain norms for PG accommodation, while retaining restrictions in A and B category colonies. Locals, however, allege that these restrictions are routinely flouted.The extent of the transformation has also raised questions about structural safety. While MCD said it was yet to ascertain whether construction or repair work was being carried out at the time of Sunday’s building collapse, locals said some work was allegedly underway in the basement.A senior MCD official said the building violated the prescribed height limit of 17.5 metres. “We are examining whether incessant rain and seepage weakened the structure or whether repair or other work may have contributed to the collapse,” the official added.Prof V K Paul, director, School of Planning and Architecture, Delhi, said, “The complete collapse with no tell-tale distress warning indicates it must have been a thoroughly unengineered building. Quite certainly, other nearby buildings must have been impacted due to the vibration triggered by the collapse. This wasn’t likely an isolated unsafe building, and safety audit of all such buildings must include whether emergency services have access to them. Let there be an instant compliance to a basic checklist before occupation is permitted.”The incident is not the first of its kind in Satya Niketan. In April 2022, two labourers were killed when a building undergoing renovation collapsed.In 2012, Delhi govt allowed residents of 45 resettlement colonies, including Satya Niketan, to obtain freehold rights by paying a prescribed percentage of the circle rate. The move gave property holders greater control over their properties and facilitated their sale, division of floors and access to bank loans.Experts say this put considerable pressure on the neighbourhood’s infrastructure. Narrow lanes now have to handle heavy pedestrian and vehicular movement, while old buildings have undergone repeated alterations and additions. Traffic congestion and waterlogging have further exposed the limitations of infrastructure designed for a much smaller population.The transformation of Satya Niketan raises concerns about other settlements in the vicinity. Areas like Kusum Pahadi, where forest and ridge land have witnessed encroachment, and Basant Gaon, located in the forest/ridge area, may face similar pressure as values of plots rise and urbanisation expands rapidly.
Article Summary: Satya Niketan, a resettlement colony in south Delhi, has undergone a dramatic transformation from a low-rise neighbourhood to one of the capital’s most densely built hubs. The shift began relatively gradually, with locals renting out rooms to students. Over time, the growing demand for accommodation turned houses into commercial rental properties.

Article Title: No rain in 122 taluks for three weeks; 50% crop losses likely in Karnataka
Article Text:
(Representative image) Karnataka is grappling with a staggering 50% downturn in agricultural and horticultural yields

Crisis in cauvery dams too





BENGALURU: With an underwhelming monsoon showing no signs of revival and rain deficit in the state set to widen in coming weeks, Karnataka is likely to lose about 50% of its agriculture and horticulture harvest.Karnataka has declared 102 of its total 239 taluks ‘drought hit’; 26 more taluks may join the list in a week.The crisis-hit districts are Mysuru, Mandya, Chamarajnagar, Hassan, Kolar and Chikkaballapura. In northern parts of the state, Haveri, Bidar and Raichur are seeing a serious drop in sowing.“As per our preliminary assessment, of the 228 taluks facing drought-like situation, 122 have seen dry spells of three weeks consecutively. This means the situation is dire for crop cultivation,” said a revenue department official.According to officials, preliminary estimates place the south-interior region as the worst hit. “While we may see some crops being salvaged along irrigated lands, those dependent on rainfall will show little or zero yield this time. We’re staring at a 50% crop loss,” said the official.Karnataka, as of the previous agriculture season, had 82.5 lakh hectares under agriculture production. This year, only 36.5 lakh hectares have seen sowing yet.Minister Eshwar Khandre said govt has assessed the state needs Rs 2,600 crore in relief measures for 101 taluks declared drought-hit. “CM Shivakumar will likely seek additional compensation from the Centre,” Khandre said.
Article Summary: Karnataka has declared 102 of its total 239 taluks ‘drought hit’ The crisis-hit districts are Mysuru, Mandya, Chamarajnagar, Hassan, Kolar and Chikkaballapura. In northern parts of the state, Haveri, Bidar and Raichur are seeing a serious drop in sowing.

Article Title: Homeopaths turn to allopathy amid job insecurity in Maharashtra, but just 10 have permission
Article Text:
Homeopaths are now practicing modern medicine after receiving pharmacology certificates.

This situation forces locals to seek cheaper and more accessible alternative practitioners.

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think about the rising number of alternative practitioners in Mankhurd? It's a necessity due to lack of access to MBBS doctors It's concerning for patient safety It reflects on the healthcare system's failures I have no opinion 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion





The country's first medical council-registered homeopath, Mankhurd-based Neha Pawar, has kept her shop closed for the past year. In its place stands a motor driving school. Pawar was given her certificate by the Maharashtra Medical Council (MMC) on Aug 3, despite severe pushback from the medical community.Maharashtra's total count of homeopaths allowed to practice modern medicine based on a one-year Certificate Course in Modern Pharmacology (CCMP) rose to ten this week, with Pawar and Mayuresh Kamble being the only two based in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. There are more than 10,000 such applicants. Experts point out that this massive demand to cross-practice stems from large-scale job insecurity.Dr Abhay Shukla, co-convener of Jan Swasthya Abhiyan, said, "We need to sympathise with them. They have years of training into something that does not work. Policies should now use whatever skills they have. The one-year pharmacology certificate course is insufficient but with rigorous training, they could be deployed in limited capacities at primary health centres."In Mankhurd's Ambedkar Nagar, Pawar's erstwhile clinic is surrounded by alternative practitioners like her. There is no MBBS doctor in sight, forcing locals to blindly trust whoever they can find.Those who do remember her recall her clinic as one of the many that opened and shut, but also a place they went to for occasional fever and cough check-ups.The area is home to many of the city's daily wage earners. Tasneem Usmani, a local pharmacist, said, "There is no option here for people. There are no MBBS doctors very close by, but others [alternative practitioners] are accessible and cheap, so they take a chance. The practitioners give their own tablets wrapped in paper."Pawar has been giving out allopathic medicines since 2017, years before she was legally permitted to do so. She told TOI that the shop is now closed for personal reasons and that she has no immediate plans to resume practice."All we check is if their registration is active with the homeopathic council and if they have any cases of negligence against them," said MMC registrar Dr Rakesh Waghmare.Her clinic was next to that of Shagufta Basha, a Unani practitioner, who said alternative medicine practitioners in the area -- such as herself, or ayurveda practitioners and homeopaths -- charge a small sum of Rs 100 and give out allopathic medicines to patients with fever, cough, typhoid and malaria. "TB patients are referred to a nearby BMC clinic. There is one MBBS doctor ten minutes away, but he is expensive for this population," she said.Dr Vijay Chavan, a pulmonologist who has treated TB patients for years in Mankhurd-Govandi, said the fees of an MBBS general physician there is Rs 200-300, so many walk into the first cheaper alternative they see, and it doesn't matter who sits there. "It is a risk and a problem, and it backfires many times with patients finally reaching doctors with some adverse reaction. But to be fair, even qualified MBBS doctors have been contributing to the haphazard use of medicines," Dr Chavan said.Inside homeopath Mayuresh Kamble's clinic at Survale Nagar, Badlapur (East), a rate card is pasted on the wall: Rs 150 for a consultation, Rs 200 for a consultation with an injection, Rs 50 for a BP check and the same charge for a dressing, Rs 100 for an injection prescribed by another doctor, and Rs 500-700 for a home visit.Most of his patients are working-class, he said. "When I started the practice here and had opened a shop in the area, there was almost nothing here. Buildings were coming up, and construction workers used to visit me for treatment."In the over an hour that TOI spent at his clinic, there were parents bringing their children with injuries for dressings, diabetes patients, respiratory distress patients, and patients complaining of fever and cough, many bringing their blood reports for advice, and even those with known high cholesterol.He looked at chest X-rays to check if one of his patients had TB or if it was a case of bronchitis. Many of his patients were people who had visited some other doctor in the recent past, farther from their homes, and landed up at his clinic because it was the closest option for a quick consultation.They also did not know that Kamble is a homeopath, though his board mentioned qualifications such as BHMS with CCMP. Homeopathy was almost entirely absent in his clinic. The medicines Kamble prescribed ranged from standard antibiotics to cough syrups, and he even considered statins for one of his patients if they did not visit a referred doctor. Throughout the time TOI spent by his desk, not a single homeopathic pill was prescribed -- barring one packet to a diabetic patient.
Article Summary: 10 homeopaths allowed to practice modern medicine based on one-year Certificate Course in Modern Pharmacology. Neha Pawar and Mayuresh Kamble are the only two based in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. Experts point out that this massive demand to cross-practice stems from large-scale job insecurity.

Article Title: 20-ft-deep well found under razed mosque in Saharanpur, ASI to examine site
Article Text:
A 20-ft-deep well found under demolished mosque in Saharanpur.





BULANDSHAHR: A day after a 70-year-old mosque inside Saharanpur collectorate premises was demolished by the district administration for allegedly encroaching upon govt land after the masjid’s appeal was rejected by the district judge’s court, a nearly 20-foot-deep well was found beneath the rubble on Sunday, raising questions about the structure’s antecedents.The discovery was made when workers, while clearing the rubble, came across a concrete slab. The slab, officials said, was unusually strong. A Pokland machine was brought in to break it, but failed to make a significant impact. Workers then used a cutter, following which a brick-lined well was found.After the discovery, officials said that the well will be examined by Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) to establish its antiquity and historical relevance.According to officials, the well is around 1.5m in diameter and nearly 20-ft-deep. Its exact age, purpose and history remain unclear, they said. Police personnel were deployed at the collectorate premises soon after the news of the discovery spread across the district.Cautioning against drawing any conclusion about the well’s origin before an expert report, Sadar SDM Subodh Kumar said, “It will be examined by ASI.Only once it’s complete, we can say how old it is...”The demolition came a year after Bajrang Dal member Vikas Tyagi raised objections to the alleged “illegal” presence of the mosque on govt land. The dispute subsequently went through the courts. On July 17, the city magistrate’s court had declared the structure an “illegal encroachment on govt land” and also ordered its occupants to pay Rs 6.4 crore in compensation.The mosque side challenged the order, but its appeal was rejected by the district judge’s court on Friday after both sides were heard and the evidence was examined.The district administration thereafter proceeded with the demolition early on Saturday.Those associated with the mosque alleged that they were not given an opportunity to approach the high court before the demolition. Advocate Babar Wasim said the mosque committee would challenge the “reckless” action before the HC.Meanwhile, the discovery of the well has now added another layer to the dispute, with the complainant claiming that it could point to an older religious structure at the site. Tyagi said: “There could have been an earlier place of worship here. Now that a well has been found, our suspicion has been strengthened... This well could be several hundred years old.”Saharanpur MP Imran Masood, meanwhile, alleged that the administration acted in “haste”. “What has happened is extremely unfortunate for the Constitution and the state’s judicial system. First, the order under which the action was taken was not a demolition order. It was only an eviction order and 22 days were still left. Yet the entire place was cleared at one go. SC and HC have repeatedly spoken about giving time before any demolition work. ”
Article Summary: The well is around 1.5m in diameter and nearly 20-ft-deep. Its exact age, purpose and history remain unclear, officials said. The well will be examined by Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) to establish its antiquity and historical relevance.

Article Title: From hesitation to habit: Why Mumbai’s women are choosing bike taxis, despite safety concerns
Article Text:
Bike taxis are gaining popularity among Mumbai commuters seeking faster and cheaper travel options.

The rules for bike taxis

# A look at the fares





MUMBAI: At 8.45am outside Andheri railway station, the monsoon-dampened air is thick with exhaust fumes, blaring horns and long queues of frustrated commuters. As autorickshaws refuse short-distance rides and buses crawl through traffic, 26-year-old finance professional Sneha Kulkarni bypasses the chaos with a few taps on her phone. Within minutes, she is riding pillion on a bike taxi towards MIDC, determined not to miss her morning meeting.Sneha is far from alone. Across Mumbai and the wider metropolitan region, women and Gen Z commuters are increasingly embracing bike taxis, reshaping long-held perceptions about urban mobility. In a city where riding behind an unfamiliar male driver was once viewed with hesitation, convenience is rapidly overcoming social barriers. The reason is simple: bike taxis save both time and money.“With fares starting at around Rs 10 per km, compared with an average of Rs 18 for autorickshaws and even higher fares for app-based cabs, the financial appeal is equally strong,” said a media professional from Nariman Point. “In South Mumbai, I’ve used bike taxis several times to go from college to the station or meet friends,” said undergraduate student Shriya Narayan.“It costs much less than a cab and gets me there faster. ”But there are risks as well. Transport analyst Vivek Pai pointed out: “Women need to recognise that motorcycles are among the most vulnerable vehicles on the road. Unlike a car, there is very little protection if something goes wrong. When booking a bike taxi, the passenger is also placing trust in an unknown rider whose driving habits and risk-taking behaviour are not known. That itself carries an element of risk.”He further advised: “Safety must remain the top priority. Both the rider and the pillion passenger should wear helmets without exception. As bike taxis become more popular, strict enforcement of helmet use and safe riding practices will be crucial, especially for women commuters.”Many commuters complain that captains rarely provide helmets to pillion riders, despite double helmets being mandatory under Mumbai’s traffic rules and required under the proposed bike taxi framework. “I’ve travelled several times by bike taxi and never received a helmet,” said rider Akshita Bhat. “With potholes and unpredictable traffic, it is a risk.”Transport officials also noted that a recommended separator pad between rider and passenger is rarely seen on operating bikes.Safety concerns have intensified following a handful of accidents involving bike taxis, including a fatal Navi Mumbai crash last year and another serious accident in Worli earlier this year. Experts said the incidents should serve as a wake-up call as the sector expands.Meanwhile, companies such as Rapido are promoting women-focused initiatives like Bike Pink, which deploys female captains exclusively for women passengers. “Bike Pink is more about making mobility more inclusive and enabling more women to choose rides with women captains,” a Rapido spokesperson said. A few women complained why the Bike Pink was slightly expensive than the normal bike taxi. Sources in bike taxi firms said that the fares were based on demand-supply formula.For frequent rider Neha Gupta, the attraction goes beyond economics. “It’s quick, readily available and honestly quite enjoyable. I don’t mind a male rider when it gets me to my destination safely and on time,” she said.Bike taxi captains say female passengers now form a significant share of their daily rides, particularly around corporate hubs such as Bandra-Kurla Complex and major transit points like Bandra and Andheri stations. Digital safeguards including live GPS tracking, SOS buttons, real-time route monitoring and trip-sharing with family members have helped build trust among women riders.The state government is now moving towards legalising bike taxis, with operators expected to pay a daily licence fee and contribute a share of each fare to a welfare fund. The momentum behind two-wheelers is gaining high-level policy backing as well.Union Road Transport Minister Nitin Gadkari recently advocated strongly for the sector, urging state governments to allow private two-wheeler owners to operate bike taxis. Pointing to the massive economic upside, Gadkari noted that liberalising bike taxi rules could unlock livelihood opportunities for nearly eight crore people, particularly across rural and semi-urban belts.* Crash helmets for riders as per permissible specifications shall be required to be provided for each ride. The helmets shall be cleaned and hygienic* All the penal provisions for traffic rule violations shall also be applicable to the bike taxis in order to ensure compliance and safety* The distance between the origin and the destination of a trip shall not be more than 15 km* Speed limit: 60 kmph* Bike taxi service providers shall provide facility in their app for women passengers to opt for a female rider and vice versa ensuring enhanced safetyKm ..........Fare1.5 km......Rs 153 km.........Rs 314 km ........Rs 416 km ........Rs 628 km ........Rs 8210 km ......Rs 10315 km.......Rs 154
Article Summary: Bike taxis are gaining popularity among Mumbai commuters seeking faster and cheaper travel options. Fares start at around Rs 10 per km, compared with an average of Rs 18 for autorickshaws and even higher fares for app-based cabs. Women and Gen Z commuters are increasingly embracing bike taxis, reshaping long- held perceptions about urban mobility.
